title: Chocolate leaf transfers
subtitle: Using real leaves as moulds to make chocolate leaves for cake decoration
excerpt: Chocolate leaves are made by painting melted chocolate onto the underside of a fresh, clean leaf, leaving it to set, then peeling the leaf away. The underside of the leaf has raised veins that transfer as a mirror image. Rose, bay, lemon, and camellia leaves all work.
sourceNotes: Chocolate leaf-casting is a well-established decorating technique taught in patisserie courses and appearing in professional confectionery manuals from the 1970s onwards. The vein-transfer principle is the same across all leaf types; the choice of leaf affects the vein detail.

recipe.batchNotes: Paint leaves in batches. Work with 20 leaves at a time so you can chill the first batch while preparing the next.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Finished chocolate leaves keep in a cool, dry place for up to a week. Place on the cake on the day.

glossaryTerms.definition: A decoration technique in which chocolate is painted onto a real leaf, allowed to set, and the real leaf peeled away to leave a chocolate replica with raised veining.

content.text: Chocolate leaves use real leaves as a mould. Paint chocolate onto the underside, chill until firm, peel the leaf away, and the

keeps the vein pattern from the original. Rose leaves give the most readable veins. Bay and camellia leaves give a thicker, more architectural result. Avoid leaves from the garden that may have been sprayed or are from toxic plants.

Wash the leaves in cold water and dry them thoroughly with a paper towel. Any moisture will cause the chocolate to seize on contact. Lay the leaves upside down (underside up) on a sheet of baking paper so you can paint them without moving them.
Melt 100 g of dark, milk, or white chocolate in a heatproof bowl over a pan of barely simmering water, stirring until smooth. Remove from the heat.

Paint a layer of chocolate onto the underside of each leaf with a pastry brush, working from the stem outward. Keep the coating to about 2 mm thick; too thin and the leaf will be fragile, too thick and the vein detail is lost.
Chill the leaves flat for 10 minutes. Apply a second coat and chill for a further 15 minutes until completely firm.

Remove from the fridge and allow the leaves to sit at room temperature for 2 minutes so the chocolate has firmed but is not cold enough to snap. Hold the chocolate leaf by the stem, peel the real leaf back from the tip in one smooth motion. Work slowly. If the chocolate breaks, the second coat was too thin or the chocolate was too warm. Transfer to baking paper and store in a cool dry place.
Paint the first coat in dark chocolate and the second in white to get a two-tone leaf. The veins show in dark against the white background.
